title: Automation and Job Displacement
body:
**Automation** removes tasks, and a whole occupation disappears only when all of its tasks go.
That distinction is what the economic block is built on. A job is a bundle of tasks, and
automation takes the ones that are routine and codifiable, leaving the rest and changing what
the job is.

That predicts which work is affected better than a manual and cognitive split does. Payroll
processing is cognitive and highly routine, so it automated early. Plumbing is manual and
highly variable, so it has not.

The historical pattern is consistent across three centuries of mechanisation:

```
total employment      recovers, and frequently grows
the distribution      does not return to what it was
the timing            recovery takes a generation, and the displaced worker
                      does not get the new job
```

The last line is the ethical content. The people who lose work and the people who gain from
cheaper output are rarely the same people, so the gain is diffuse and the loss is concentrated.
[[Utilitarianism]] handles this poorly, since the total is positive and the totals hide the
distribution, and it is the standard case for showing why the framework needs a distributional
supplement.

What is new in the current round is the range of tasks affected and the speed. A model that
drafts, summarises and classifies reaches work that previous automation could not, and it
arrives over years where mechanisation arrived over decades.
